subject: MGMT160
title: Managing in the Age of AI: The Future Manager's Toolkit

questions.stem: Explain why AI can be confidently wrong.
options: It predicts plausible answers from patterns, not from understanding
It is programmed to lie when it does not know the answer, to keep users happy
It always copies the first website it finds, which may be out of date
It cannot read numbers, so every figure in its answers is a guess
questions.why: AI predicts plausible text; plausible is not the same as true. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Identify three things AI can do well, according to the chapter.
options: Analyse information, recognise patterns and generate content
Feel emotions, take responsibility and hold values
Know your team's history, motivate people and lead them
Replace managers, judges and doctors in routine decisions
questions.why: AI analyses, predicts and generates. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Describe the 'role' part of a strong prompt.
options: Telling the tool who it is acting as, such as an adviser to a café manager
The user's job title, so that the tool knows how senior the reader is
The name of the AI company and the version of the tool being used
The password and account details needed to log in to the tool
questions.why: Role, context, task, audience and format, constraints. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Explain 'garbage in, garbage out' for prompts.
options: A vague prompt produces generic text that helps no one
AI cannot read long prompts, so the user should keep requests to one line
All AI output is garbage
Only short prompts work, because the tool ignores anything after the first sentence
questions.why: Brief a tool as you would brief a new assistant. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Describe what the human keeps in the organising function when AI builds the schedule.
options: Fairness — what the algorithm is told to optimise
Nothing, because the algorithm has the staff list and the rules
The spreadsheet in which the schedule is stored
The clock and the opening hours of the business
questions.why: Fairness is a human setting. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Describe what the human keeps in the controlling function when AI reads the dashboards.
options: The monitoring line and the judgement about what the numbers mean
Nothing — AI controls everything once the KPIs have been set
Only the password to the dashboard and the list of users
The office keys and the physical security of the building
questions.why: AI reads patterns; the human decides the line. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Explain why AI raised the floor faster than the ceiling in the customer-service study.
options: It carried the know-how of the best agents to the newest ones
It replaced the experts
It made everyone slower, but the newest agents were slowed down least
It only helped managers, who used it to coach the newest agents
questions.why: Largest gains went to the least experienced. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Describe the risk inside the jagged frontier.
options: People trust AI on tasks outside its ability and do worse than without it
AI refuses hard tasks, so people have to do them without any help
AI is slow on easy tasks, so people lose time waiting for simple answers
There is no risk, because the frontier is clearly marked in the tool
questions.why: Confident help arrives exactly where the tool is wrong. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Describe the lesson of the lawyer who asked the AI whether its cases were real.
options: Checking with the same tool is not checking — verify against an independent source
The AI was right and the court was mistaken about the cases
Lawyers should never use AI for any part of their work
The court was wrong to sanction lawyers who relied on a licensed tool
questions.why: It said yes; the cases were invented. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter says the professional who signs is responsible.
options: Submitting work under your name makes you accountable for its truth
The AI company is responsible, because its tool produced the error
Nobody is responsible, because the error was made by a machine
The reader is responsible for checking anything they rely on
questions.why: The professional who signs is responsible. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Describe the 'bias in hiring' fault line.
options: Trained on yesterday's hires, AI can apply yesterday's prejudices at scale
AI always hires the best person, because it has no personal prejudices
AI cannot read CVs that are written in an unusual format
AI prefers older applicants because they have longer work histories
questions.why: Bias at scale, politely. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Describe the 'accountability' fault line.
options: Nobody can say 'the AI decided' to a customer, court or team
AI is always accountable, because every decision is logged in the system
Accountability no longer matters with software
Only the IT department is accountable, because it installed the system
questions.why: Assist, never decide. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Describe good use of AI for drafting.
options: Draft with AI, then apply your own judgement and checks before using it
Copy the draft without reading it, because reading it defeats the time saving
Let AI send the draft itself, so that the manager is not delayed
Never draft with AI, because the text will not sound like the manager
questions.why: Replace the manual work, never the judgement. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Explain why communication stays the manager's monopoly.
options: No one is inspired by software
Managers type faster than AI tools can generate text
AI cannot write messages that are grammatically correct
Software cannot send email without a human pressing the button
questions.why: People follow people. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's prediction for managers.
options: Managers who use AI will replace managers who don't
All managers will be replaced within a generation
Nothing changes, because management has never depended on technology
Only managers without degrees will be replaced
questions.why: AI absorbs the administrative layer. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Explain why the human core of management becomes more valuable.
options: Direction, motivation, ethics and judgement are what remains after routine work is automated
Humans will be rarer in organisations, so each one will be paid more
Salaries always rise when new technology is introduced
AI needs managers to switch it on and keep it running
questions.why: The human core becomes more valuable, not less. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Describe the 'AI, human-checked' decision type.
options: AI does the routine layer and a person sets the rules and handles exceptions
AI decides everything alone and a human reads the report afterwards
Humans do everything by hand and AI checks the result for errors
AI checks the human's decision and overrules it when the data disagrees
questions.why: Shift scheduling is the chapter's example. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Determine the missing part in the prompt 'Write a report on customer service for the manager, one page, table format'.
options: Context — the situation and data the report is about
Audience — who the report is written for
Format — how the report should be laid out
Constraints — the length and limits of the report
questions.why: Audience, format and constraints are there; context is missing. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Select the strongest prompt for a staffing plan.
options: 'You are advising a 20-person café. Using last Ramadan's hourly sales, propose a staffing plan per hour for Iftar week, as a table, with one risk per day'
'Make a staffing plan for our café for Ramadan. We are usually very busy at Iftar and we never seem to have the right number of staff, so please think carefully about it'
'Help with Ramadan — we need to plan our staff for the busiest week of the year and we want to avoid the problems we had last year with long queues and tired staff'
'Give me ideas for how a café should manage its staff during Ramadan, including the hours, the breaks, the number of people and anything else we should think about'
questions.why: Role, context, task, audience/format, constraints. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a prompt that gives role, context and task but no format. Determine the likely result.
options: Usable content in an unpredictable shape that needs re-work
Perfect output, because role, context and task are the parts that matter
No output at all without a format
A table, because tools default to tables when no format is given
questions.why: Format tells the tool how to deliver. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Classify AI reading 300 customer reviews and listing the top five complaints.
options: Controlling — monitoring; the human keeps the judgement
Leading — motivating the staff with customer feedback
Organising — assigning complaints to departments fairly
Planning — setting the goal for next month's reviews
questions.why: Reading signals is controlling support. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Determine the right behaviour for an experienced agent given a new AI tool.
options: Use it where it is strong and keep checking it where it is weak
Trust it completely, because it has read more cases than any agent
Refuse it, because experienced agents do not need help
Use it only for personal email, where mistakes do not matter
questions.why: The jagged frontier: know where the tool is wrong. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a consultant who did worse with AI on a task outside its ability. Determine the lesson.
options: Trusting the tool outside its frontier is worse than working without it
AI should never be used by consultants, whose work depends on judgement
The consultant was not smart enough to use the tool properly
AI is useless for professional work and should be kept for routine tasks
questions.why: Dell'Acqua et al.: confident help where the tool is wrong. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Select the study finding that supports giving AI tools to new hires first.
options: Productivity gains were largest for the least-experienced agents
Experts gained the most, because they knew how to prompt the tool
Nobody gained, but new hires complained less about the work
Customers complained more when they were served by new hires with AI
questions.why: AI carried the best workers' know-how to the newest. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Determine what a manager must do before sending an AI-drafted letter to a client.
options: Check every fact and figure against a source the tool did not write
Ask the AI whether the letter is correct and send it if it says yes
Send it if it reads well, because fluent text is a sign of accurate content
Add a disclaimer that AI was used and send it without further checks
questions.why: Anything filed, sent, published or decided gets checked. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Classify a report that cites a statistic the AI invented.
options: The signer's responsibility — the professional who signs is accountable
The AI's fault only, because it produced the statistic
Nobody's fault, because the error was made by a machine
The reader's fault for not checking the statistic before relying on it
questions.why: Mata v. Avianca: the lawyers were sanctioned. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Classify an AI that rejects job applicants no human ever sees.
options: Dangerous — AI deciding, not assisting
Reasonable — it saves recruiters' time for the strongest candidates
Reasonable — AI has no bias, so its rejections are fairer than a human's
Required by law in large organisations to ensure consistent treatment
questions.why: A life-shaping decision needs a human owner. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Determine the ethical question to ask about any AI use at work.
options: Legal? fair? who is harmed — including those the model never showed you? the public test?
Is it fast enough to save the team time?
Is it cheaper than doing the work by hand?
Is it popular with the staff who will use it?
questions.why: Run the four questions. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Classify 'use AI to summarise a 40-page report, then read the key sections yourself'.
options: Good use — summarising with judgement kept
Bad use — trusting the summary blindly
Bad use — hiding the use of AI from the reader
Bad use — letting the AI decide what matters in the report
questions.why: Summarise, then apply judgement. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Determine who should decide a customer refund when the policy is unclear.
options: Human — judgement in a new situation
AI — it knows the policy and applies it consistently
AI, human-checked — the system decides and a person signs
Nobody — unclear cases should be refused until the policy is rewritten
questions.why: Judgement with real stakes stays human. See §9.8.
